transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-05
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 64 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Ethan Morales (Redwood SE); Priya Nair (CTO, Stratus); Omar Hassan (Platform Eng); Lina Gomez (ML Infra)
Recorded: yes (auto)

Summary:
We did a deep technical walk-through of Redwood's KV slab allocator behavior under write-heavy long-context workloads. Focus areas: slab affinity, writeback throttling, background paging, prefix churn, and diagnostics to reproduce an eviction cascade. Agreed next steps: run a targeted staging experiment (writeback enabled vs disabled) and share telem.

Topics covered:
- Slab allocator design and intentional hot-shard affinity
- Writeback vs immediate eviction tradeoffs
- Paging thresholds and KV hole filling
- Long-context streaming interactions with continuous batching
- Telemetry fields (last-touch, prefix-hash, slab-id, eviction-reason)

Action items and quick recap included below.

--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate, auto transcript with occasional mishears) ---
[00:00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll kick us off. quick intros please.
[00:00:06] Priya: hi i'm priya, cto at stratus, we run the convai product and we're seeing periodic latency spikes during long streaming sessions.
[00:00:15] Omar: and i'm omar, platform, i've got the logs and some flamegraphs in the shared doc.
[00:00:20] Ethan: cool, thanks. quick note, today we're going to role play a few eviction scenarios, show slab allocator internals, and propose a writeback trial.

[00:02:40] Ethan: first, high-level: our KV store uses a slab allocator to map prefix keys to fixed-size slots, slabs are pinned to worker threads for locality, that prevents cross-NUMA thrash. in heavy write or append workloads, the hot prefix can saturate a slab and the allocator will either evict least-recently-used slots in that slab or trigger a background writeback to spill to disk, depending on the config.
[00:03:12] Priya: can you spell out the writeback path again? like where does it persist and what durability guarantees exist?
[00:03:22] Ethan: sure; by default writeback persists to the local NVMe on the inference node and then we optionally copy to object storage asynchronously. durability is best-effort unless you enable persistent write-through which will sync to blobstore per checkpoint - that costs latency.

[00:05:05] Omar: the pattern we saw: long context sessions create very long KV chains; when a new session reuses a prefix, we get a burst of cache misses that cause a bunch of slots to be allocated, then evicted when the slab fills, then paging - that interleaves with GPU stall and spikes latency.
[00:05:39] Ethan: yep, that's classic prefix reuse churn. a key part is the slab affinity: if a prefix hashes to the same slab across requests, it stays hot on that worker - good for cache hit rate - but if you have many prefixes colliding, that slab becomes a hot spot and you see eviction churn.

[00:07:50] Lina: i want to call out our workload is mostly conversational with ~8-10k token windows occasionally reaching 30k with streaming. we prefer low tail latency at the cost of slightly higher p50.
[00:08:05] Maya: that helps, okay. so tradeoffs: more slabs (smaller slab size) reduces per-slab collision but increases metadata and lookup cost; bigger slabs reduce metadata overhead but amplify hot-slab eviction.

[00:09:30] Priya: is there an option to bias allocator to favor read-heavy prefixes? like a hot-read write-cold policy?
[00:09:40] Ethan: we have an adaptive policy flag—readAffinityMode—that keeps read-dominant prefixes resident by lowering their eviction score and adjusting the LRU window, versus writeAffinityMode which favors rapid churn. it's experimental but we can toggle it per-customer.

[00:11:20] Omar: about paging, our nodes have NVMe saturated at ~80% during test. when writeback kicks in we see higher disk IOPS and those async writes sometimes block KV housekeeping which delays evictions and creates a backlog.
[00:11:42] Ethan: right, that's a known emergent behavior: writeback can cause background I/O that interferes with in-memory compaction jobs. mitigation: rate-limit writeback and isolate IO queues via cgroups or dedicated NVMe partitions. we suggested IO QoS settings in the doc.

[00:13:50] Priya: how do you recommend we reproduce an eviction cascade in staging so it's deterministic?
[00:14:02] Ethan: best practice script: 1) fixed prefix set of ~300 prefixes hashed to same slab id via our prefix-hash shim, 2) ramp N concurrent streams to simulate mix of long-context append and random reads, 3) force slab occupancy to 95% then toggle writeback on/off and measure p95/p99 tail. i'll share the script.

[00:15:40] Maya: quick interjection — we added a small telemetry field last quarter: "eviction-reason" with codes (0=slab-full,1=ttl,2=manual-free,3=io-backpressure). have you surfaced that in your logs?
[00:15:55] Omar: yes, we see a lot of code 0 and code 3 during spikes. code 3 surprised us — we thought backpressure was only on heavy writes.
[00:16:10] Ethan: code 3 is the allocator detecting sustained IO latency and proactively throttling writeback, converting immediate evictions into a deferred channel. it's designed to avoid compaction storms but it can increase memory pressure short-term.

[00:18:25] Lina: okay, what about continuous batching — our app uses low-latency streaming and we rely on small batch sizes; does batching interplay with slab behavior?
[00:18:35] Ethan: yep, continuous batching means more interleaved KV touches. small batches reduce average latency but increase per-token metadata churn. in practice we tune batch windows and set an eviction hysteresis so slots touched in the last X ms get a grace period.

[00:21:00] Priya: security question: if we enable local NVMe writeback, what's the KMS/HSM flow for encrypting persisted KV blobs?
[00:21:10] Maya: we support envelope encryption. keys can be customer-managed via KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or HSM on-prem). nodes encrypt before writing to NVMe and key retrieval is gated by IAM. we also produce audit events for each key use.

[00:23:44] Omar: on network, will writeback produce egress to our blobstore and trigger VPC egress charges? also need to confirm it respects egress firewall rules.
[00:23:55] Ethan: yes if you enable persistent offload to blobstore. default config keeps copies local and optionally uploads during off-peak windows. we respect customer VPC egress and can do S3-compatible endpoints in-region to avoid cross-region egress.

[00:26:20] Priya: we ran the sample trace you provided and saw a pattern where hot prefix rotates every 12 seconds and eviction spikes follow at ~18s intervals, which aligns with the slab lease expiry in our config. can we tweak lease to smooth that?
[00:26:36] Ethan: lease (our slab sticky timeout) is tunable. increasing lease reduces churn but increases memory residency of cold items. one idea: implement lease ramping during warmup then decay gradually. we have an RFC for that.

[00:29:40] Maya: let's role play a remediation — suppose we have an urgent customer SLA breach. immediate mitigation steps we recommend?
[00:29:49] Ethan: 1) enable readAffinityMode if workload is read heavy, 2) temporarily increase slab count to reduce collision, 3) throttle continuous batching depth so writes are smoothed, 4) if NVMe io is saturated, disable writeback and increase memory headroom until off-peak persists complete.
[00:30:10] Omar: disabling writeback seems risky for durability though.
[00:30:16] Ethan: agreed, that's why it's a short-term mitigation and you should capture the writeback backlog before disabling so you can rehydrate safely. also we have an option to divert writeback to a secondary node in the same zone which reduces local contention.

[00:32:55] Lina: curious about metrics — which new telemetry fields do you want us to collect for the trial?
[00:33:05] Ethan: collect slab-id, slot-alloc-count, last-touch-ms, eviction-reason, writeback-queue-length, nvme-iops, nvme-latency, batch-window-ms, prefix-hash, and active-stream-count. we provided a prom exporter snippet in the shared doc.

[00:36:20] Priya: any guidance on quantization interacting with kv cache? we use int8 models for inference to save GPU memory.
[00:36:31] Ethan: quantization affects tokenization and KV cache sizes because lower precision can change serialized KV blob size. generally int8 reduces model memory but KV footprint is independent; however, some model runtimes pack KV differently for quantized kernels which can slightly change evict patterns. we'll add tests for your model build.

[00:39:12] Omar: i want to test the writeback rate-limiter setting — what knobs exist?
[00:39:20] Ethan: three knobs: target-iops, bytes-per-second, and concurrent-writeback-threads. we suggest starting with conservative bytes/s and 2 threads then ramp. also set IO scheduler on node to deadline for more predictable latency.

[00:42:00] Priya: do you support stateful mirroring across nodes so if a slab node fails another keeps a warm copy?
[00:42:10] Ethan: we support an optional warm-mirror mode — it keeps an async replica of hot slabs in a buddy node; it's not fully synchronous but reduces cold-start penalties on failover. it adds network overhead though.

[00:44:55] Maya: quick note on cost/latency trade-off: warm-mirror + persistent write-through gives best availability but increases cost. Stratus needs to prioritize tail latency over p50, so we recommended warm-mirror with reduced slab size and readAffinityMode.

[00:48:30] Priya: let's talk about instrumentation — you mentioned a CSV export we'll feed our engineers to plot.
[00:48:39] Ethan: yes, we'll send a csv with event timestamps, slab-id, eviction-reason, nvme-lat, and p99 latency sample. please run the script during your high-load window.

[00:51:02] Omar: one thing: in the sample traces i saw a weird "slot recycle" event that the UI labeled as speaker 1 but the code shows it as manual free. is that a UI mismatch?
[00:51:14] Ethan: sometimes the auto-transcription for the event log maps internal codes — there's a small mapping bug. we'll fix the UI label; the underlying event is manual-free (code 2) triggered by a compaction job.

[00:54:20] Lina: if we do the writeback experiment, what success criteria should we define?
[00:54:30] Maya: suggested success criteria: p99 tail reduced by >=25% during the same throughput, no sustained increase in NVMe latency over baseline, and no new data-loss incidents. also define an acceptable cost delta.

[00:57:05] Priya: timeline — we want initial data in 1 week and then a follow-up technical call.
[00:57:15] Maya: sounds good. we'll share the scripts and toggles today and ethan will prepare the replay runbook.

[00:58:40] Ethan: i'll also add the slab-debug build we used (it's non-prod only) to the shared drive with instructions to enable verbose telemetry.

[01:00:10] Omar: do you have any benchmarks comparing writeback-on vs writeback-off for workloads like ours?
[01:00:20] Ethan: we have internal benchmarks across convai-like workloads; i will attach the summary CSV. high-level: writeback-off reduces NVMe pressure and short-term latency but increases transient memory demand; writeback-on reduces long-term memory but can create IO spikes if not rate-limited.

[01:02:00] Maya: ok let's close with next steps — we'll run the staging experiment, share telem, and reconvene next Thursday.
[01:02:12] Priya: thanks everyone, appreciate the thoroughness.
[01:02:20] Maya: thanks all. bye.
